strengths: Significance: The fixed forward horizon is a useful theoretical advance. Theorem 4.1 separates the required perturbation time from the desired sampling accuracy for norm-subgaussian targets. Under additional smoothness assumptions, Theorem 5.1 also improves the accuracy dependence of the sampling complexity relative to the stated comparator.

Originality: Theorem 4.2 provides a valuable score-confinement and clipping argument that converts L2 estimation accuracy into the exponential-moment control needed for inexact Langevin dynamics. The contribution supplies new understanding of an existing predictor-corrector approach.

Soundness: The main analysis has a coherent structure: Gaussian smoothing yields a quantitative log-Sobolev inequality, inexact Langevin dynamics controls initialization error, and Wasserstein stability propagates this error through the reverse ODE. The explicit decomposition distinguishes initialization, score estimation, and early-stopping errors.

Presentation and theoretical reproducibility: The roles of the algorithmic parameters are explained clearly, and the proof sketches are supported by detailed appendices. The manuscript acknowledges the stronger loss and distinguishes the continuous and discrete settings. No material research-ethics concerns are apparent from the theoretical analysis and synthetic examples.
weaknesses: The claim that Wasserstein convergence requires only the usual L2 training loss needs qualification. Equations (4.3)–(4.4) retain the potentially large stability factor I_tau, and the convergence discussion on page 8 requires additional control of the estimator's one-sided Lipschitz constants. Small L2 error does not imply this control. Theorem 4.2 also requires endpoint accuracy b(T1), which is not guaranteed by a small integrated loss alone. An explicit combined convergence statement should make these requirements and the limiting procedure precise.

The final assertion of Lemma 4.8 is false as stated. Take d=1, p a point mass at sqrt(2/3), and t=log(sqrt(2)). Both stated time conditions hold, but p_t=N(1/sqrt(3),1/2), giving D_KL(gamma || p_t)=5/6−log(2)/2≈0.4868, exceeding the claimed 1/3. This auxiliary bound needs correction. The main theorems impose stricter time bounds, so the example does not directly refute their conclusions.

The scope of the guarantees is narrower than some headline wording suggests. The broad Wasserstein result concerns a continuous-time ODE and retains dimension-dependent stopping and stability terms; logarithmic dependence applies to the prescribed forward horizon, not the complete error or computational complexity. The discrete result instead concerns a reverse SDE and assumes uniformly Lipschitz true scores through time zero, excluding the singular targets motivating part of the Wasserstein analysis.

The practical efficiency claims have limited evidence and the numerical illustrations are insufficiently reproducible. Figure 1 provides three toy examples without comparisons at matched computational cost or measurements of training savings. The manuscript does not specify the chosen T1 values, model and training configuration, solver settings, sample counts, Wasserstein estimation procedure, or meaning of the error bars. Furthermore, the unclipped experiments do not measure the exponential-moment loss, so they do not establish that clipping is unnecessary. These shortcomings limit the empirical claims, although the theoretical results remain the principal contribution.
